Synchronize the existing cancellation test with real virtualized data requests.

## Description

Only eight lines are added to `CancelsOutdatedRefreshes_Async`; no shipping code, test asset, assertions, browser defaults or package versions change.

Wait for the existing loading attribute before releasing the initial provider, then wait for actual loaded items before scrolling. After each native `scrollTo`, wait for a new non-null pending-placeholder window before issuing another scroll. Preserve every exact scroll-position wait and the final cancellation-count assertion.

This prevents the initial scroll from being clamped before data establishes the scroll extent, and prevents all five scrolls from coalescing into one provider request. There are no sleeps or injected observer/provider callbacks.

**Boundary:** Virtualize and its native browser observers own request production. Existing loading/placeholder DOM observes that real path; the existing cancellation count observes the material result. Permanent coverage remains the existing Server/WASM Selenium cases. A synthetic callback test would bypass the lost-scroll/coalescing preconditions.

**Red/green evidence**

Against current main `a6110c23cf`, the unchanged two-case run initially passed, then a fresh repeat failed `ServerVirtualizationTest.CancelsOutdatedRefreshes_Async` at the exact scroll-position wait, line 420. The WASM case passed both baseline runs; no WASM baseline failure is claimed.

An intermediate counter-instrumented test-asset variant passed the cancellation cases but failed the server sizing control (7/8 passed). That approach was discarded entirely. The final change observes existing DOM and has no test-asset diff.

All commands ran after `source activate.sh` in the same immutable AL4 Chrome image used by #70689 (`sha256:42d8a12504aa39a3c6e336a43937320a7086ad87701dd7b5d1e1c7cc6a8ddd30`), SDK `12.0.100-alpha.1.26557.102`, Chrome 158, default viewport and untrimmed Release applications.

Build: **passed**, zero warnings/errors.

```sh
dotnet build src/Components/test/E2ETest/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-restore -c Release -p:UseMonoRuntime=false -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:TestTrimmedApps=false -m:2 -v:q
```

Final targeted run: **Passed: 8, Failed: 0, Skipped: 0**, exit 0. Both Server/WASM cancellation cases plus `RerendersWhenItemSizeShrinks_Async`, `RerendersWhenItemSizeShrinks_Sync` and `EmptyContentRendered_Async` controls passed.

```sh
dotnet test src/Components/test/E2ETest/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-build -c Release -p:UseMonoRuntime=false -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:TestTrimmedApps=false --filter "FullyQualifiedName~CancelsOutdatedRefreshes_Async|FullyQualifiedName~RerendersWhenItemSizeShrinks_Async|FullyQualifiedName~RerendersWhenItemSizeShrinks_Sync|FullyQualifiedName~EmptyContentRendered_Async" --logger "trx;LogFileName=green-dom.trx" --results-directory /evidence/virtualization-repair-green
```

Five additional fresh runs: **Passed: 2, Failed: 0, Skipped: 0** each, all exit 0. This is a bounded stability sample, not proof across hosts/load.

```sh
for attempt in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  dotnet test src/Components/test/E2ETest/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-build -c Release -p:UseMonoRuntime=false -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:TestTrimmedApps=false --filter FullyQualifiedName~CancelsOutdatedRefreshes_Async --logger "trx;LogFileName=green-$attempt.trx" --results-directory /evidence/virtualization-repair-repeat || exit $?
done
```

Every exported final TRX was parsed: exact expected names/counts, unique execution/test identities, matching definitions, all executed/passed and zero skipped/failed/aborted/pending. The expected failing baseline was separately parsed.

Formatting and diff checks: **passed**, exit 0.

```sh

git diff --check
```

Issues.Title: Synchronize virtualization cancellation E2E test with provider progress
Issues.Body:
Follow-up to #70767 and the merged AL4 browser migration #70689.

`ServerVirtualizationTest.CancelsOutdatedRefreshes_Async` can issue its first scroll while the asynchronous container is still only 500px tall. Chrome clamps that scroll to zero; later loading does not reissue it. Waiting only for scrollTop also permits several scrolls to coalesce before native observers start separate provider requests.

Reproduced against current main `a6110c23cf` in the same immutable AL4/Chrome image as CI: the first unchanged Server/WASM run passed both cases, while the next run passed WASM and failed Server at the exact scroll-position wait (`VirtualizationTest.cs:420`). This is a timing race, not a deterministic failure or an AL4-only claim. Earlier real-browser producer evidence: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/70767#issuecomment-7116289198

Acceptance: synchronize the existing Selenium test with the real initial provider/loading state, loaded data before scrolling, and a distinct pending window after each native scroll. Preserve all existing scroll/cancellation assertions, including count > 0. No fixed sleeps, synthetic observer callbacks, shipping behavior changes, test quarantines, or browser-default changes.

# [Blazor] Enable WebAssembly boot resource retries by default

Let the runtime retry failed Blazor WebAssembly boot resource downloads.

## Description

Remove Blazor's `enableDownloadRetry: false` override so the runtime can recover from a cached empty or error response for a fingerprinted boot resource (dotnet/runtime#136527). Healthy cache hits still use the cache; a failed `force-cache` fetch can be retried with `cache: "reload"` without disabling integrity checks. This also enables ordinary bounded runtime retries. Download concurrency is unchanged, and apps can still opt out through `configureRuntime`.

### Validation

- `npm run build --workspace src/Components/Web.JS` — passed for Debug and Release on current `main` with the fix, after rebuilding the SignalR workspaces.
- From `src/Components/Web.JS`, `..\..\..\node_modules\.bin\eslint.cmd -c .\src\.eslintrc.js .\src\Platform\Mono\MonoPlatform.ts` — passed on current `main` with the fix.
- Before moving the one-line fix onto current `main`, ran the reporter's cache-recovery scenario with local Playwright/Chrome and a published .NET 12 standalone app. The original bundle stayed stuck on a cached empty HTTP 200 or 404 after origin repair. The patched bundle performed exactly one `reload` fetch with integrity still enabled and rendered on Mono. The next boot used the healthy cache without another origin request, and explicit opt-out preserved the no-retry behavior. CoreCLR passed the download assertions, but end-to-end rendering was not validated with that older checkout's Blazor bundle. The browser repro was not rerun after moving onto current `main`.

Fixes #69488

This change and PR description were prepared with GitHub Copilot.

Issues.Title: Open redirect possible in Blazor template `IdentityRedirectManager.RedirectTo`
Issues.Body:
#69197 added a `//` check to `IdentityRedirectManager.RedirectTo` in the Blazor Web App template, but the check can be bypassed by prefixing the payload with the app's own base URI. Any input that isn't a well-formed relative URI goes through `NavigationManager.ToBaseRelativePath`, which strips the base URI. The remainder (`//evil.example`, or `\/evil.example`, which `System.Uri` normalizes to `//`) is then passed to `NavigateTo` without further validation, and `System.Uri` resolves it as a link to another host.

### Repro

1. Create an app with `dotnet new blazor -au Individual` (SDK 11.0.100), run it on `http://localhost:5091` and register and confirm a user.
2. Log in via `/Account/Login?ReturnUrl=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A5091%2F%2F%2Fevil.example`.
3. The response is `302 Location: http://evil.example/`. The backslash variant `http://localhost:5091/\/evil.example` behaves the same.

### Affected

All template pages that redirect to `ReturnUrl` (Login, LoginWith2fa, LoginWithRecoveryCode, ExternalLogin, Register, PasskeyUpgrade). The same code is on main, release/10.0, release/9.0 and release/8.0.

Issues.Title: Harden identity redirect handling in Blazor template
Issues.Body:
`IdentityRedirectManager.RedirectTo` in the Blazor Web App template validated the raw redirect string. That check could be bypassed because `ToBaseRelativePath` strips the app's base URI and leaves a network-path reference such as `//evil.example` (or `\/evil.example` after backslash normalization), which `NavigateTo` then resolves to another host.

This change resolves the URI against the app's base URI the same way `NavigationManager` does and only allows destinations whose absolute URI is within the base URI. The app root without a trailing slash (for example `/app?x=1`) is also allowed, matching `ToBaseRelativePath`. The path base is compared ordinally, so a case-different path such as `/APP/` is rejected, while scheme and host stay case-insensitive because `System.Uri` normalizes them. Anything else falls back to the base URI, so rejected input now redirects to the home page instead of throwing.

Fixes #70797

Issues.Title: CacheView: async parent initialization can leave cache fills pending and hang subsequent requests
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

A CacheView rendered by a component with async `OnInitializedAsync` can leave its cache entry pending forever.

The first request completes successfully. Following requests for the same cache key hang until the client times out. This reproduces with static SSR, the default in-memory CacheView store, and no additional packages or interactive components.

Delaying creation of the CacheView until the parent's async init finishes avoids the problem.

In an isolated reproduction:
- Without the guard: request 1 completed in approximately 200 ms; requests 2 and 3 each exceeded a two-second client timeout.
- With the guard: all three requests completed in approximately 50–60 ms and replayed identical cached markup.
- With the guard: 30 concurrent cold requests completed without timeouts.

### Expected Behavior

CacheView should tolerate its parent rerendering after asynchronous initialization.

The first request should populate the cache entry, and following requests should complete using the cached output. 

A parent re-render should not abandon a pending cache fill or cause later requests to hang.

### Steps To Reproduce

Reproduction: https://github.com/jsneedles/cacheview-async-init-repro 

Run:
`dotnet run --project CacheViewRepro.csproj --no-launch-profile`

The application starts a local server and automatically exercises both variants:

- `plain`: the first request succeeds; subsequent requests time out.
- `guarded`: all requests succeed and cached markup remains unchanged.
- 30 concurrent guarded cold requests: all succeed.

The only relevant difference is whether CacheView is created before or after the parent's asynchronous initialization completes.

### Exceptions (if any)

_No response_

### .NET Version

11.0.100

### Anything else?

- OS: macOS 26.6, ARM64 (osx-arm64)

Also reproduced in an AWS-deployed Linux arm environment, so the issue is not limited to macOS or local development. The isolated reproduction above was run locally on macOS ARM64.

Issues.Title: [Feature Request] Allow NuGet Package Manager to Filter Updates by Target .NET Version
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

I'm currently developing and maintaining projects targeting **.NET 10 LTS**, but since the release of .NET 11, Visual Studio's NuGet Package Manager frequently suggests newer package versions that are not compatible with my project's target framework.

The problem is that the **Updates** tab does not provide a clear option to exclusively display package updates that are compatible with the project's target .NET version.

When checking for updates, I want to see the latest available version of each package that my project can actually use, regardless of the package's major version number.

For example:

- If a package version `11.0.1` supports .NET 10, it should be suggested.
- If a package version `11.0.1` requires .NET 11, it should not be suggested.
- If the latest compatible version is `10.0.4`, that should be the suggested update instead.

Currently, this requires manually selecting individual packages, opening their version dropdowns, and identifying which versions are compatible with my project.

For solutions containing numerous NuGet dependencies, this becomes unnecessarily repetitive, frustrating, and time-consuming.

**I want Visual Studio to automatically identify and suggest only the latest NuGet package versions that are compatible with my project's target framework, regardless of their major version numbers.**

### Describe the solution you'd like

I would like Visual Studio's NuGet Package Manager to introduce a **"Show Compatible Updates Only"** option that automatically filters available package updates based on the project's target framework.

Rather than simply suggesting the latest published package version, Visual Studio should determine the latest version that is actually compatible with the project.

### Proposed Features

- **Automatic Framework Detection:** Detect the project's target framework, such as `net10.0`.
- **Compatibility-Based Filtering:** Only suggest package versions that support the project's target framework.
- **Latest Compatible Version:** Suggest the newest compatible package version, regardless of its major version number.
- **Exclude Incompatible Updates:** Hide package versions that require a newer .NET framework than the project targets.
- **Update All Integration:** Ensure the **Update All** functionality only installs compatible package versions.
- **Solution-Wide Support:** Allow this preference to be applied across all projects within a solution.
- **Persistent Settings:** Remember the developer's filtering preferences between Visual Studio sessions.

### Example

Given a project targeting:

```xml
<TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
```

And the following hypothetical package versions:

| Package Version | Supported Frameworks | Should Be Suggested? |
|---|---|---|
| 10.0.2 | .NET 10 | ✅ Yes |
| 10.0.4 | .NET 10 | ✅ Yes |
| 11.0.0 | .NET 10, .NET 11 | ✅ Yes |
| 11.0.1 | .NET 11 only | ❌ No |
| 11.0.2 | .NET 11 only | ❌ No |

**Expected suggested update:**

```text
11.0.0
```

Even though newer versions exist, `11.0.0` is the latest version compatible with the project's target framework.

If no 11.x versions supported .NET 10, Visual Studio should suggest `10.0.4` instead.

### Suggested UI

Add a simple checkbox or toggle within the **Updates** tab:

```text
NuGet Package Manager > Updates

[x] Show compatible updates only

Target Framework: .NET 10

[x] Apply to all projects in solution
```

When enabled:

1. Visual Studio detects the project's target framework.
2. NuGet evaluates available package versions for compatibility.
3. Only compatible updates are displayed.
4. The latest compatible version is automatically selected.
5. **Update All** updates packages to their latest compatible versions.

### Multi-Targeting Support

For projects targeting multiple frameworks:

```xml
<TargetFrameworks>net10.0;net11.0</TargetFrameworks>
```

Visual Studio should only suggest package versions compatible with **all targeted frameworks**, unless the project uses framework-specific package references.

### Alternative Solutions Considered

**1. Manually selecting compatible versions**

This is unnecessarily repetitive when managing numerous NuGet packages.

**2. Restricting package major versions**

This is not an ideal solution because a package's major version does not necessarily correspond to its minimum supported .NET framework.

For example, a package version 11.x might still fully support .NET 10 and should therefore remain eligible for updates.

**3. Using external tools or command-line utilities**

Developers managing dependencies directly through Visual Studio should not need additional tools to filter incompatible updates.

### Expected Outcome

When I open the **Updates** tab for a .NET 10 project, I want Visual Studio to automatically suggest the latest package versions that support .NET 10.

**I do not want to restrict packages to version 10.x. I want to restrict suggestions to versions that are compatible with my project's target framework.**

This would make package management significantly more efficient and allow developers to use **Update All** without manually identifying incompatible package versions.

### Additional context

This feature would be particularly beneficial for developers maintaining applications on **.NET LTS releases**.

For example, I currently use **.NET 10 LTS** and intend to remain on that target framework while continuing to receive the latest compatible NuGet package updates.

With the release of .NET 11, some package updates may require the newer framework, while others may continue to support .NET 10.

The NuGet Package Manager should distinguish between these cases automatically.

### Important Distinction

**Package major version and .NET framework compatibility are not the same thing.**

A package numbered `11.x` may support .NET 10, while another package with the same major version may require .NET 11.

The filtering should therefore be based on the package's actual supported target frameworks and NuGet compatibility rules, rather than its version number.

Ideally, compatibility checks should also account for:

- The project's target framework.
- The package's supported target frameworks.
- Framework compatibility and fallback rules.
- Package dependency requirements and version constraints.
- Multi-targeted projects.
- Central Package Management (`Directory.Packages.props`).

### Why This Matters

This feature would:

- Eliminate unnecessary manual version selection.
- Prevent incompatible package updates from being suggested.
- Allow developers to receive newer major package versions when they remain compatible.
- Make **Update All** more reliable.
- Improve dependency management for .NET LTS projects.
- Reduce time spent maintaining large solutions.

### Final Thoughts

I prefer managing NuGet packages directly through Visual Studio's graphical NuGet Package Manager.

I should not have to manually inspect each package version to determine whether it supports my project's target framework.

**The NuGet Package Manager should simply suggest the latest compatible version of each package, regardless of whether that version is 10.x, 11.x, or higher.**

A **"Show Compatible Updates Only"** option would be a significant quality-of-life improvement for Visual Studio developers.

Issues.Title: [blazor] Sections: support opt-in aggregation of section content
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

Reusable components may need to contribute dialogs or toasts to one location in the layout. With Blazor sections, when multiple `SectionContent` instances target the same outlet, only the last registered provider renders. A separate outlet per component instance requires the layout to know about those instances, rather than providing a shared destination.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add an opt-in way for one `SectionOutlet` to render all active `SectionContent` instances for its name or ID. Keep the existing last-provider-wins behavior as the default. For example (API shape illustrative):

```razor
<SectionOutlet SectionName="Dialogs" Mode="SectionOutletMode.Aggregate" />
```

The design should define a deterministic order, preserve the identity of unaffected providers when another is added or removed, and retain each provider's logical parent and cascading values. Provider registration order and per-provider keys are possible approaches; the API and implementation need design.

### Additional context

My Recollections app uses a shared `Dialogs` placeholder near the end of [HeadLayout.razor](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Commons/Layouts/HeadLayout.razor):

```razor
<ChangePasswordModal @ref="ChangePasswordModal" />
<TemplatePlaceholder Name="Dialogs" />
<Toast @ref="ThemeToast" />
```

Its [placeholder implementation](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.Components/Components/TemplatePlaceholder.cs) stores multiple providers and renders each fragment (excerpt):

```csharp
private HashSet<TemplateContent> content = new();

// ...
foreach (TemplateContent fragment in content)
{
    builder.AddContent(i, fragment.ChildContent);
    i++;
}
```

The app's `HashSet` does not specify output order; a built-in solution should define one. The [content component](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.Components/Components/TemplateContent.cs) registers itself and removes itself on disposal.

The [Map component](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.Components/Components/Map.razor) supplies its search and map-type modals to `Dialogs`. [MapPage](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Entries/Pages/MapPage.razor) uses `Map` and separately contributes a toast:

```razor
<Map @ref="mapComponent" Markers="@Markers" MarkerSelected="OnMarkerSelectedAsync" EnableCountriesView="true" EnableCurrentLocationButton="true" CurrentLocationError="OnCurrentLocationErrorAsync" />

@* ... *@

<TemplateContent Name="Dialogs">
    <Toast @ref="CurrentLocationErrorToast" />
</TemplateContent>
```

Other components contribute independently, for example [ShareLinkButton](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Commons/Components/ShareLinkButton.razor):

```razor
<TemplateContent Name="Dialogs">
    <Toast @ref="Toast" />
</TemplateContent>
```

This can be useful for placing dialogs outside containers that clip or constrain them. These examples are source-based; simultaneous rendering has not been verified in the running app.

Related: #61434 concerns multiple outlets for one name, the opposite direction; #51864 discusses appending `HeadContent`. The proposed aggregation API has not been prototyped.

Issues.Title: [blazor] Sections: support fallback content on SectionOutlet
Issues.Body: ### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem. A layout often needs a default for a section that pages can override. Blazor's sections do not currently expose a way to declare fallback content directly on `SectionOutlet`. A layout can register a default `SectionContent` before the page content, but its precedence depends on registration order. ### Describe the solution you'd like Allow an outlet to declare fallback content, rendered when no matching `SectionContent` is active. When a provider appears it replaces the fallback; when the last provider is removed, the fallback is shown again. For example (API shape illustrative): ```razor ``` The parameter name and its interaction with a templated outlet would need design work. The framework already has an internal default-provider mechanism (`SectionContent.IsDefaultContent`), used by `HeadOutlet` for the default title; this request is for a public, outlet-level way to express a fallback. ### Additional context In my Recollections app, the [layout declares a `MobileTitle` placeholder](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Commons/Layouts/HeadLayout.razor) with a document-title fallback: ```razor @foreach (var content in contents) { @content.ChildContent } ``` The [placeholder implementation](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.Components/Components/TemplatePlaceholder.cs) renders `EmptyContent` when no content is registered: ```csharp if (content.Count == 0) { builder.AddContent(0, EmptyContent); return; } ``` A page such as [Calendar](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Entries/Pages/Calendar.razor) overrides the fallback: ```razor Calendar ``` Detail pages also use [InlineTitleEdit](https://github.com/neptuo/Recollections/blob/ffb9a480d25612e164c1ae838acc118be4d11644/src/Recollections.Blazor.UI/Entries/Components/InlineTitleEdit.razor) to supply an interactive title: ```razor @EditTemplate(true) @EditTemplate(false) ``` Related: #52477 also asks for empty-section content. This issue focuses on declaring fallback content on the outlet and its behavior as providers come and go. The proposed API has not been prototyped.

Issues.Title: Fix lazy-loaded root component resolution in Blazor WebAssembly
Issues.Body: ## Description This PR improves lazy-loaded assembly handling during Blazor WebAssembly root component activation. It ensures that assemblies required by a root component—including assemblies containing its parameter types—are available before Blazor resolves the component and deserializes its parameters. When a page contains a WebAssembly component from a lazy-loaded assembly, the server can prerender its content, but the browser must download that assembly before activating the component. Previously, root component processing could attempt to resolve the component type before the assembly was available. The same failure could occur when the component itself was already available but one of its parameter types belonged to a lazy-loaded assembly. ## Root cause Root component registration and update processing attempted to resolve component types and deserialize parameters before the required lazy-loaded assemblies were downloaded. This caused activation failures, including when transitioning from prerendered content to WebAssembly interactivity. Asynchronous assembly loading also requires root component updates to remain ordered so later batches do not overtake initial activation or earlier updates. ## Fix changes - Defer initial root component registration when required assemblies are unavailable, and load them before resolving and rendering the components. - Discover required assemblies from component markers, including parameter type assemblies. - Preload missing lazy assemblies before resolving initial and subsequent root component operation batches. - Clear cached type-resolution results after loading assemblies. - Preserve root component update ordering while assemblies download. - Notify JavaScript when a batch fails without acknowledging unsuccessful additions or updates, while preserving removal processing. - Exclude the serialized render-fragment sentinel from parameter assembly loading. ## Before fix ## After fix ## Tests ### Unit tests - Deferred registration when a required parameter assembly is unavailable. - Startup when no root components require deferred registration. - Descriptor resolution for removal-only batches and unknown assemblies. - Required assembly discovery for components and parameters. - Exclusion of only the serialized render-fragment sentinel. - Filtering of already-loaded assemblies and preservation of unknown-assembly errors. ### End-to-end tests - Lazy-loaded component and parameter assemblies with prerendering enabled and disabled. - Initial page loads and enhanced navigation. - Navigation while a lazy assembly download is pending. - Recovery after a rejected lazy assembly download. Fixes #58818

Issues.Title: Fix RDG delegate generation for params, optional parameters, and named delegates
Issues.Body: ### Description Fixes #69755 This PR addresses Request Delegate Generator (RDG) failures when route handlers are mapped using delegate types that carry additional signature information beyond the target method itself. Investigation showed that RDG recreates delegate casts from the target method signature rather than preserving the original delegate type used at the mapping site. As a result, delegate-specific semantics such as `params` modifiers, optional/default parameter values, and custom named delegate types can be lost during code generation, leading to invalid generated code or runtime `InvalidCastException`. To resolve this, the generator now captures and preserves the original route handler delegate type when it can be safely referenced. Delegate compatibility is validated before code generation, and unsupported scenarios continue to fall back to the existing RDG002 diagnostic behavior. The fix ensures that: - `params` delegate handlers preserve their original delegate signature. - Delegates with optional/default parameter values continue to behave correctly. - Custom named delegates are emitted using their declared type. - Keyword-named delegates are emitted using escaped identifiers. - Unsupported or inaccessible delegate types continue to fall back to RDG002 without generating invalid code. No public API changes were introduced as part of this change. ### Validation / Investigation As part of the investigation: - Reproduced the reported delegate-cast scenarios from the issue. - Verified failures involving `params` handlers and delegate types with optional/default parameters. - Investigated RDG delegate type resolution and code generation paths. - Updated the generator to preserve route handler delegate types when compatible. - Added fallback validation to ensure unsupported delegate types continue producing RDG002 diagnostics. - Issues.Body: # Handle malformed codes in Identity account links ## Description Account links can sometimes get changed when they're copied or wrapped in an email. For example, a period might accidentally be included at the end of the code. Currently, a malformed code can throw a `FormatException` and return a 500 response when someone opens a password-reset, email-confirmation, or email-change link. This PR handles that decoding error in Identity UI V4 and V5 and in the Blazor Web App template with Individual authentication. ### Before ### Changes included - Catch `FormatException` when decoding the account-link code. - Keep the existing behavior for valid links and other Identity operations. - Add regression tests for invalid-length codes and valid codes with a trailing period. - Cover missing and unknown users, valid links, and account-state preservation. Fixes #70070

Issues.Title: Design proposal: QuickGrid column options customization and active filter indicator
Issues.Body:
# Design proposal: QuickGrid column options customization and active filter indicator

<!--
This template is useful to build consensus about whether work should be done, and if so, the high-level shape of how it should be approached. Use this before fixating on a particular implementation.
-->

## Summary

QuickGrid's default column options buttons offer limited customization for accessible labels and active-state styling. Applications need a way to communicate active options, such as filters, without duplicating the default header template.

The design decision is whether to document the existing styling workaround, add only direct button attributes, or also provide a built-in indicator. This draft describes the third option; the design review recommends documenting the workaround first and considering an attributes-only API before introducing a built-in indicator.

## Motivation and goals

- Users of grids with multiple filters cannot tell which filters are applied without opening each column's options popup.
- The original custom-header approach required reproducing the default header markup and isolated title styling. A later `Class` + CSS workaround avoids replacing the header for visual styling alone.
- That workaround cannot directly supply an accessible name or other attributes on the default options button. This is the strongest motivation for direct button customization.
- `ColumnOptions` can contain any options UI, not only filtering. Applications should choose labels that describe their own options and state.
- A class-only parameter cannot supply accessible labels or other button attributes. Attribute customization should follow the established QuickGrid/Paginator pattern.
- Developers should control whether active state appears as the built-in dot, custom styling, or no visual indicator.
- Applied filter state belongs to the application, whether it filters a local query or supplies criteria to an `ItemsProvider`. QuickGrid does not infer state from options content.
- Styling and labels can render in static HTML; opening options and updating state through interactions require an interactive grid.
- Keep regression coverage focused on distinct behavior and the two button-rendering branches.

The originating request is [dotnet/aspnetcore#54537](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54537). Its [existing workaround](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54537#issuecomment-2058536956) uses the column's `Class` with application CSS.

## In scope

- Preserve the default header, sorting controls, and options popup while allowing an application-defined visual cue and accessible label.
- Keep the cue and label tied to the application's applied filter, not merely text being edited.
- Document the existing no-API styling workaround for comparison.
- Add `ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes` as an optional `IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>` parameter on `ColumnBase<TGridItem>`.
- Support `ColumnOptionsActive` for application-controlled active state.
- Support `ColumnOptionsButtonClass` for additional button styling, combining its trimmed value with `col-options-button` and classes supplied through `ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes`.
- Apply the attribute dictionary to both default options-button variants.
- Let applications supply `aria-label`, CSS classes, and other button attributes.
- Keep `col-options-button` and application-supplied button classes, with QuickGrid owning popup-expanded state and click handling.
- Retain the built-in active indicator when `ColumnOptionsActive` is true and the attribute dictionary does not contain a `class` key.
- Treat an explicitly supplied `class` as an override of the built-in active class. An empty class suppresses the built-in indicator without clearing the active state.
- Consolidate managed class-composition coverage and retain Selenium coverage for one alignment from each rendering branch.

## Out of scope

- Widening framework CSS selectors with `::deep` to change custom-header styling. This CSS-only minimum is considered below but is not part of the current proposal.
- Automatically detecting filters from arbitrary options content.
- Adding filter-change events or changing the application's filtering logic.
- Replacing the `ColumnOptions` or `HeaderTemplate` rendering contracts.
- Automatically rendering the default options button inside a custom `HeaderTemplate`.
- Changing sorting, pagination, virtualization, or filter-state persistence.
- Defining a general design system or adding new theme tokens.
- Unrelated framework, stylesheet, or test-infrastructure refactoring.

## Risks / unknowns

- **API shape remains unsettled:** the attributes-only recommendation removes the need for a separate button-class parameter and avoids prescribing an indicator. The three-parameter alternative offers a built-in cue but has overlapping customization paths.
- An explicit `class` overrides only the automatically added `col-options-active` token, not `col-options-button` or `ColumnOptionsButtonClass`. This precedence must be clear to consumers.
- An ordinary styling class therefore also suppresses the built-in indicator. This is an intentional but surprising rule in the current draft, not a settled convention. An attributes-only API or a separately agreed visibility contract would avoid that coupling.
- Empty attribute classes intentionally suppress the built-in indicator. Attributes without a `class` key, such as a label-only dictionary, must not suppress it.
- Applications own accessible labels describing their options and active state. The generic options title alone does not communicate active state.
- Filter-active state and popup-open state are independent: closing the popup must not clear a filter, and opening it must not mark a filter active.
- Consumer classes are merged without dropping `col-options-button`. Consumers may supply `aria-label` and override the generic `title`; QuickGrid should retain ownership of `type="button"`, its options click handler, and `aria-expanded`.
- Conflicting reserved attributes should not override those QuickGrid-owned values. The implementation must be checked against this proposed contract: the current local markup places `type` before attribute splatting, so it does not yet enforce the proposed type precedence.
- A custom `HeaderTemplate` owns its own button, attributes, and styling.
- Attribute composition can allocate a combined class string when a non-empty attribute class is supplied. Reuse the existing shared helper, avoid copying dictionaries during rendering, and make no claim of allocation-free customization.
- The current implementation has been inspected from source, but build, browser red/green validation, and performance measurements remain pending.
- The broader choice between a built-in filter indicator and an attributes-only API remains subject to maintainer/API-review agreement.

## Examples

### Apply and clear a filter

This interactive component distinguishes edited input from the applied filter. Applying "Ada" shows one row and changes the button's label and cue; clearing restores both rows and the inactive presentation.

```razor
@using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.QuickGrid

<QuickGrid Items="@FilteredPeople">
    <PropertyColumn Property="@(p => p.Name)"
                    ColumnOptionsActive="@IsFilterApplied"
                    ColumnOptionsButtonClass="name-options"
                    ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes="@(IsFilterApplied ? _activeAttributes : _inactiveAttributes)">
        <ColumnOptions>
            <label>
                Name filter
                <input type="search" @bind="_draftFilter" @bind:event="oninput" />
            </label>
            <button type="button" @onclick="ApplyFilter">Apply</button>
            <button type="button" @onclick="ClearFilter">Clear</button>
        </ColumnOptions>
    </PropertyColumn>
</QuickGrid>

@code {
    private string _draftFilter = string.Empty;
    private string _appliedFilter = string.Empty;
    private readonly IQueryable<Person> _people =
        new[] { new Person("Ada"), new Person("Grace") }.AsQueryable();

    private bool IsFilterApplied => !string.IsNullOrEmpty(_appliedFilter);

    private IQueryable<Person> FilteredPeople => IsFilterApplied
        ? _people.Where(person => person.Name.Contains(_appliedFilter))
        : _people;

    private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> _inactiveAttributes =
        new Dictionary<string, object> { ["aria-label"] = "Name options" };

    private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> _activeAttributes =
        new Dictionary<string, object> { ["aria-label"] = "Name options (filter active)" };

    private void ApplyFilter()
    {
        _appliedFilter = _draftFilter.Trim();
    }

    private void ClearFilter()
    {
        _draftFilter = string.Empty;
        _appliedFilter = string.Empty;
    }

    private sealed record Person(string Name);
}
```

Host this component interactively, for example in an Interactive Server page. Because these dictionaries contain no `class` key, the built-in indicator follows the applied filter. Editing input alone does not change the rows, cue, or accessible label.

### Application-defined styling

In the preceding example, the active dictionary can instead contain:

```csharp
private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> _activeAttributes =
    new Dictionary<string, object>
    {
        ["class"] = "name-filter-enabled",
        ["aria-label"] = "Name options (filter active)"
    };
```

The rendered classes are `name-filter-enabled col-options-button name-options`. The application defines `.name-filter-enabled` styling; QuickGrid does not additionally impose `col-options-active`. `ColumnOptionsActive` can remain true.

### No visual indicator

Use an empty class while retaining a descriptive label:

```csharp
private static readonly IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> _activeAttributes =
    new Dictionary<string, object>
    {
        ["class"] = string.Empty,
        ["aria-label"] = "Name options (filter active)"
    };
```

The rendered classes are `col-options-button name-options`. The application keeps the active state and accessible label without the built-in dot.

### Existing workaround without new APIs

Using the same filtering state and apply/clear controls, replace the column's proposed parameters with:

```razor
<PropertyColumn Property="@(p => p.Name)"
                Class="@(IsFilterApplied ? "name-filter-applied" : null)">
    <ColumnOptions>
        <label>
            Name filter
            <input type="search" @bind="_draftFilter" @bind:event="oninput" />
        </label>
        <button type="button" @onclick="ApplyFilter">Apply</button>
        <button type="button" @onclick="ClearFilter">Clear</button>
    </ColumnOptions>
</PropertyColumn>
```

Application CSS in a global stylesheet can style the existing button:

```css
.quickgrid .name-filter-applied .col-options-button {
    background-color: #ffe08a;
}
```

The column class changes the header and cell classes; the selector targets only the options button. This preserves the default header and needs no new API, but cannot assign a state-dependent accessible name to that button.

<!--
# Detailed design

It's often best not to fill this out until you get basic consensus about the above. When you do, consider adding an implementation proposal with the following headings:

Detailed design
Drawbacks
Considered alternatives
Open questions
References

If there's one clear design you have consensus on, you could do that directly in a PR.
-->

## Detailed design

The following API and rendering rules describe the proposed developer experience.

### Public API

```csharp
public abstract partial class ColumnBase<TGridItem>
{
    [Parameter]
    public bool ColumnOptionsActive { get; set; }

    [Parameter]
    public string? ColumnOptionsButtonClass { get; set; }

    [Parameter]
    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object>? ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes { get; set; }
}
```

`ColumnOptionsActive` defaults to false. `ColumnOptionsButtonClass` and `ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes` default to null. The dictionary is an explicit button parameter, not a `CaptureUnmatchedValues` parameter.

### Rendering and precedence

| Input | Result |
| --- | --- |
| All parameters at defaults | `col-options-button`; generic options title; no explicit `aria-label`. |
| `ColumnOptionsButtonClass` supplied | Append its trimmed value to `col-options-button`. |
| Active, with no attributes or no `class` key | Add `col-options-active`; retain the built-in indicator. |
| Active, with a non-empty attribute class | Combine that class with the base class and `ColumnOptionsButtonClass`; do not automatically add `col-options-active`. |
| Active, with an empty attribute class | Keep the base class and `ColumnOptionsButtonClass`; omit the built-in active class. |
| Label-only attributes | Render the supplied label without changing active styling. |
| Consumer `title` or `aria-label` | Render the application-supplied value; otherwise retain the generic title and no explicit label. |
| Consumer `type`, `onclick`, or `aria-expanded` | The proposed contract keeps QuickGrid's button type, options handler, and popup state authoritative; implementation alignment is pending. |
| Popup opens/closes | QuickGrid updates `aria-expanded` independently of active styling and supplied attributes. |
| Custom header template | The template owns its options UI; default-button customization is not applied. |

Use the existing `AttributeUtilities.CombineClassNames` helper rather than a new composition mechanism. Retain the built-in CSS rule and `--quickgrid-column-options-active-color` fallback for consumers that use the built-in indicator.

### Validation plan

- The following tests describe the current three-parameter candidate, not an approved test contract. If attributes-only is selected, remove tests for built-in active state and class-based suppression.
- `ColumnOptionsButtonCssClass_PreservesExistingClasses`: focused parameterized cases for defaults, custom button classes, active state, explicit custom overrides, and empty-class suppression.
- `ColumnOptionsButtonCssClass_LabelOnlyAttributesPreserveActiveIndicator`: verify that attributes without a class do not disable the indicator.
- `ColumnOptionsIndicatesActiveFilter`: exercise real filter apply/clear, default and custom labels, built-in/custom/suppressed indicator transitions, rendered classes and computed pseudo-element appearance, and popup-expanded state.
- Run the Selenium scenario for `Start` and `Right`, covering the two distinct button-rendering branches rather than all five equivalent alignment values.
- Exercise unchanged defaults, combined classes, custom title and label, and conflicting reserved attributes. The no-attributes case must retain the default button class and options behavior.
- Extend the browser scenario to edit a draft filter, prove rows and state do not change before Apply, then apply and clear it. Assert row contents/counts, indicator appearance, and accessible name together.
- Check opening and closing the popup independently of applying or clearing filters; verify the type remains `button` inside a form and reserved attribute conflicts do not replace the options handler or expanded state.
- Require the changed assertions to fail for the expected reason without the corresponding change and pass with it. These executions remain pending; source inspection and whitespace checks are not runtime verification.

## Drawbacks

- Separate active-state, class, and attribute parameters create overlapping customization paths.
- Consumers must understand the explicit class-override rule.
- Applications must supply meaningful labels and any custom styling themselves.

## Considered alternatives

- **Docs-only workaround:** document column `Class` plus application CSS. This already solves visual styling without copying the header and adds no API; it does not expose direct button labels or other attributes.
- **Attributes only:** add only `ColumnOptionsButtonAttributes`, merge classes, and let applications supply their own state-dependent styling and labels. This is the design review's recommended API candidate if maintainers agree direct customization is needed. It avoids redundant class parameters and class-triggered indicator suppression, but applications supply indicator CSS.
- **Built-in indicator plus attributes:** the current draft adds active-state and button-class parameters alongside attributes. It offers a default cue but introduces overlapping controls and the disputed class-override rule. Defer the built-in dot and theme token if maintainers prefer the simpler first version.
- **CSS selector widening with `::deep`:** could make isolated title styles available to custom headers, but still requires replacing the header and does not provide or infer applied-filter state. This addresses custom-header styling rather than direct default-button customization.
- **Always additive classes:** preserves existing class composition but does not let applications suppress the built-in active class while keeping the active parameter true.
- **Separate indicator opt-out parameter:** makes suppression explicit but adds another public parameter when an attribute override can provide the capability.
- **Automatic filter detection:** arbitrary options content does not provide a reliable filtering contract; application-controlled state is explicit.
- **Custom header templates only:** already possible, but requires duplicating the default header UI for button customization.

## Open questions

- Is documenting the existing workaround sufficient, or is direct default-button customization needed for accessible names and other attributes?
- If a new API is justified, should the first version expose attributes only and defer the built-in indicator?
- If a built-in indicator is accepted, should its visibility use an explicit contract rather than the presence of a consumer class?
- Does API review accept the explicit attribute-class override contract and final public API shape?
- How should the implementation enforce the proposed reserved-attribute contract, particularly button type precedence?
- Do the targeted managed and browser tests pass, including red/green checks, with the required repository SDK and browser assets?

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Title: System.Collections.Immutable dll being replace by Microsoft.Net.Compilers
Issues.Body:
I have referenced `system.collections.immutable.dll` from the nuget package and I also have the nuget package installed for `Microsoft.Net.Compilers`. Everything works fine in my local but when I push my code to bamboo, in the runtime I get `Could not load file or assembly 'System.Collections.Immutable, Version=1.2.3.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a' or one of its dependencies. The located assembly's manifest definition does not match the assembly reference. (Exception from HRESULT: 0x80131040)`

When I checked logs on bamboo when it generates the artifacts, I can see that initially it copied the correct dll here:

`build    04-Apr-2019 03:20:33      Copying file from "E:\agt01\ENS-EB580-JOB1\Bin\Packages\System.Collections.Immutable.1.5.0\lib\netstandard1.0\System.Collections.Immutable.dll" to "E:\agt01\ENS-EB580-JOB1\Binaries\Release\\temp\Web\_PublishedWebsites\MyService\bin\System.Collections.Immutable.dll"`.

but then at some point, it replaced this dll with this: `build    04-Apr-2019 03:20:33      Copying file from "E:\agt01\ENS-EB580-JOB1\Bin\Packages\Microsoft.Net.Compilers.1.0.0\tools\System.Collections.Immutable.dll" to "E:\agt01\ENS-EB580-JOB1\Binaries\Release\\temp\Web\_PublishedWebsites\MyService\bin\System.Collections.Immutable.dll".`

How can I make sure that bamboo does not replace this dll and just uses it from the nuget package installed?

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019" (#1078)

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

Issues.Title: Nesting bug
Issues.Body:
The is a problem nesting embedded resources.  I was experimenting with nesting .cshtml files using the existing rules and did this:

Modal.cs (bootstrap modal web component)
   -> Modal.cs.cshtml (it's view file)

`Modal.cs.cshtml` is set to Embedded Resource, and clearly shows it, but is completed IGNORED by the build process (simply open the DLL in a text editor [such as Notepad++] and scroll to the bottom and look for text).  If I rename the file to "Modal.cshtml" instead it works perfectly fine!  :/  I don't think whether or not a file is embedded should have and role in excluding a file from being embedded so this seems like a bug to me.

Yes, I'm aware of upcoming nesting controls in v15.6, but I'm not able to install it yet, and regardless, this should work fine, so it should be looked into nonetheless.

Just to add: I'm using wild-cards to include the file.  If I explicitly add it I get this:

`Duplicate 'EmbeddedResource' items were included. ...`

So it's clearly found.  It's obviously something up with the build process not finding the nested file.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Nesting bug" (#1066)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

> Update: The ASP.NET Core 2.3 end of support date was updated from April 7, 2027 to April 13, 2027 to align with the Microsoft servicing release cycles.

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

## Current support policy

ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages (latest patched version only) are currently [supported](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/platform/support/policy/aspnet#dotnet-core) on .NET Framework, following the support cycle for those .NET Framework versions. After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

## Impact of end of support

After ASP.NET Core 2.3 reaches end of support:

- No new security updates will be issued for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- Continuing to use an unsupported version may expose your applications to security vulnerabilities.
- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.
- The ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages will be deprecated.

## Upgrade recommendation

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

To help with the upgrade process, we recommend using [GitHub Copilot modernization](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/porting/github-copilot-app-modernization/overview), which provides AI-powered assistance to help you analyze, plan, and execute your migration to a modern .NET version.

Issues.Body:
Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

## Implementation

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

- Triggers on `issues.opened` and `issues.labeled` events with "Breaking change" label
- Creates issue in docs repo with:
  - Title: `[Breaking Change] <original title>`
  - Body: Link to source issue, full context
  - Labels: `breaking-change`, `aspnet/Announcements`
- Posts comment on source issue with link to docs issue

## Duplicate Prevention

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating
- Concurrency control keyed on issue number

## Error Handling

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search
- Search failures → proceed with creation (fail open to avoid missing docs)
- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

## Setup Required

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

## Security

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**

var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**

using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`
